title: The Hajj by air
hookLine: steamships then planes turn the long road to Mecca into days

lines: A ROOF LIKE A FIELD OF TENTS.
cards: At the airport in Jeddah there is a terminal built for one purpose.

Its roof is a field of white peaks, like a great camp of tents, and under it, in the season of Hajj, planes unload pilgrims in white cloth from every corner of the world. Some flew overnight. Some changed planes twice.

A grandmother from Dhaka, a nurse from Lagos, a retired teacher from Ohio, all walking out into the heat a day after leaving home. Their great-grandparents, if they went at all, went by camel, by foot, by ship.

teach.h: ON FOOT AND ON EVERY LEAN CAMEL.
teach.b: The Qur'an calls people to the pilgrimage and pictures how they will come: "They will come unto thee on foot and on every lean camel; they will come from every deep ravine." For a long time, that's how it was.
Caravans crossed deserts from Cairo and Damascus. Travelers walked a long way, and some never came home; tradition remembers the road as part of the worship.
Then the road changed. Steamships began carrying pilgrims across the Indian Ocean from India and Java to the port of Jeddah, crowded and often dangerous, but faster.
Later came the airplane, and the long road shrank to a flight. Here's the turn worth noticing.

teach.h: FOR HIM WHO CAN FIND A WAY.
teach.b: The Qur'an makes Hajj a duty "for him who can find a way thither." Planes widened that way.
A pilgrimage that could once take the work of a lifetime became something a nurse in Lagos could save for and do in her annual leave. And yet the rites themselves didn't shrink.
Once they arrive, pilgrims still walk around the Ka'ba, still go between the hills, still stand at Arafat, still sleep under the sky at Muzdalifah.
The plane gets you to the gate; the circling and the walk between the hills are still done step by step.
Days, not years, to arrive; but the same days, once you're there, as every pilgrim before.

how: Pilgrims today usually fly to Saudi Arabia for Hajj, often arriving through Jeddah or Medina, and then perform the rites in and around Mecca on foot and by bus, wearing the same simple white garments.

practice: Think of someone who made a long journey for their faith, any faith: a grandparent who went on Hajj, a friend who drives two hours to a church, temple or gurdwara.
Picture their bags, their tired feet, the moment they arrived, and then the pilots, cooks, drivers and families at home who made it possible.
Hold each one for a breath and silently thank them, and if you pray, pray for travelers in your own way.
